claims.text: The FeCoNiCrAl powder feedstock has a particle-size range of 15–45 μm.
Conventional thermal spraying of this feedstock produces insufficient coating thickness.
Conventional thermal spraying produces some as-sprayed oxidation.
Switching to optimized cold spray will increase FeCoNiCrAl bond-coat thickness relative to conventional thermal spraying.
The resulting coating thickness will exceed a purported 15–45 μm coating-thickness baseline.
Cold spraying will preserve coating integrity.
Cold spraying will limit as-sprayed oxidation relative to conventional thermal spraying.
Optimizing particle velocity maximizes particle impact energy.
Enhanced particle kinetic energy promotes denser, mechanically interlocked coating buildup.
Increasing cold-spray particle velocity improves particle deposition and coating buildup through greater impact momentum.
The lower thermal exposure of cold spray reduces oxidation relative to conventional thermal spraying.
High temperature, oxygen concentration, and powder surface area promote in-flight oxidation during thermal spraying.
Cold spraying preserves the BCC phase present in AlFeNiCoCr powder.
The cold-sprayed coating will have a homogeneous microstructure with minimal oxide inclusions.
The intervention should remain effective during subsequent high-temperature service, including aero-engine service.
Effectiveness depends on feedstock quality and particle-velocity optimization.
Extreme substrate geometries or non-ideal gas conditions may limit effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The 15–45 μm value is introduced as the powder feedstock particle-size range but is later treated as a coating-thickness baseline or feedstock-limited coating-thickness range. Particle size and deposited coating thickness are different quantities.
